210	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
211	
212	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
213	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
214	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
215	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
216	
217	## Symptoms of a skipped step
218	
219	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
220	
221	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
222	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
223	
224	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
225	
226	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
227	
228	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
229	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
230	
231	Two more facts help you read a run:
232	
233	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
234	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
235	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
236	
237	**prompt cache**
238	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
239	
240	**interrupt**
241	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
242	
243	**stop of the process**
244	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
245	
246	**automatic permission check**
247	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
248	
249	## The Bash tool and waits
250	
251	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
252	
253	- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
254	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
255	
256	## Long commands
257	
258	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
259	
260	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
261	
262	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
263	
264	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
265	
266	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
267	
268	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
269	        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
270	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
271	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
272	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
273	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
274	        done
275	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
276	    }
277	
278	If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.
279	
280	- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
281	- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.
282	
283	## Stopping processes
284	
285	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
286	
287	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
288	
289	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
290	
291	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
292	
293	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
294	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
295	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
296	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
297	
298	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
299	
300	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
301	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
302	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
303	
304	**seeding**
305	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
306	
307	**base build**
308	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
309	
310	**old code**
311	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
312	
313	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
314	
315	## Finding or building a base build
316	
317	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
318	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
319	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
320	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
321	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
322	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
323	
324	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
325	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
326	      ant compileAll
327	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
328	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
329	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
330	
331	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
332	
333	## Seeding a worktree
334	
335	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
336	
337	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
338	
339	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
340	
341	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
342	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
343	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
344	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
345	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
346	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
347	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
348	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
349	
350	## Running the old code
351	
352	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
353	
354	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
355	
356	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
357	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
358	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
359	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
360	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
361	
362	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
363	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
364	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
365	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
366	
367	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
368	
369	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
370	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
371	
372	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library and prints its errors: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count. Where an early stage of the checker finds errors in an api or a component, the checker skips its overloading and return-type checks there. So the count misses the errors of those checks there, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
5	
6	The code of this area is in these directories:
7	
8	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
9	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
10	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
11	
12	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
13	
14	## What the two paths share
15	
16	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
17	
18	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
19	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
20	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
21	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
22	
23	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
24	
25	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
26	
27	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
28	
29	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
30	
31	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
32	
33	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
34	
35	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
36	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
37	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
38	
39	It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
40	
41	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
42	
43	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
44	
45	## What the code generator does
46	
47	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
48	
49	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
50	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
51	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
52	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
53	
54	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
55	
56	## The run time
57	
58	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
59	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
60	
61	## Natives
62	
63	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
64	
65	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
66	
67	## Traps of the compiled path
68	
69	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
70	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
71	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
72	
73	## The checker's gaps
74	
75	`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.
76	
77	- Overloads: the checker reads no bounds of static parameters when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types. So it refuses `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects, and walk loads it (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
78	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
79	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
80	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
81	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
82	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
83	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

137	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about a minute. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. 139	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

168	# The interpreter (walk)
169	
170	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
171	
172	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
173	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
174	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
175	- `glue/`: the natives.
176	
177	## How walk evaluates a program
178	
179	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
180	
181	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
182	
183	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
184	
185	## Where a fix of walk belongs
186	
187	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
188	
189	- coercion;
190	- chained comparisons;
191	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
192	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
193	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
194	
195	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
196	
197	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
198	
199	## What walk checks
200	
201	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
202	
203	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
204	
205	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and message, "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", for these pairs:
206	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
207	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length;
208	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations nor a generic one beside a plain one;
209	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
210	
211	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
212	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
213	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
214	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
215	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
216	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
217	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
218	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
219	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
220	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
221	- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
222	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
223	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
224	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
225	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
226	
227	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
228	
229	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
230	
231	- adds an overload;
232	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
233	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
234	- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`.
235	
236	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
237	
238	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

240	## Natives
241	
242	The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.
243	
244	To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
245	
246	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
247	    return new FortressError(f);
248	
249	A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.

269	# Writing a test
270	
271	**gated test**
272	: Test that the gate's suites run.
273	
274	**green**
275	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.
276	
277	**red**
278	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.
279	
280	**`XXX` test**
281	: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.
282	
283	## A test program
284	
285	A test program has this form:
286	
287	    component Name
288	    export Executable
289	
290	    (* declarations *)
291	
292	    run(): () = do
293	        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
294	    end
295	
296	    end
297	
298	- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
299	- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
300	- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`, for values of any type. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
301	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
302	- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.
303	
304	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
305	
306	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
307	
308	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
309	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
310	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
311	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
312	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.
313	
314	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
315	
316	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
317	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
318	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
319	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series, by the comment in `OtherCompilerJUTest.java`. Put no new test there.
320	
321	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
322	
323	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
324	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
325	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
326	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
327	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
328	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
329	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
330	
331	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. For example:
332	
333	    tests=EqualityRung1
334	    link
335	    run
336	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
337

339	
340	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
341	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
342	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.

348	
349	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
350	
351	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
352	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. 2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 1,800 tests in four tracks at once, in about 9 to 11 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 500 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in under a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

60	
61	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
62	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
63	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
64	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
65	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
66	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.

68	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
69	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

139	# Committing and pushing
140	
141	**scratch**
142	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
143	
144	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
145	
146	## What to commit
147	
148	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
149	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
150	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
151	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
152	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
153	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
154	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
155	
156	## How to commit
157	
158	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
159	
160	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
161	
162	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
163	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
164	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
165	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
166	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
167	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
168	
169	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
170	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
171	
172	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
173	
174	## Pushing
175	
176	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
177	
178	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
179	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
180	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
181	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
182	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
183	
184	         git push origin main
185	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
186	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
187	
188	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
189	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
190	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
191	# The report and the record
192	
193	## What every report holds
194	
195	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
196	
197	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
198	
199	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
200	
201	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
202	
203	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
204	
205	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
206	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
207	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
208	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
209	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
210	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
211	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
212	
213	## At a point to report
214	
215	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
216	- Then finish the work.
217	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
218	
219	## Timings and citations
220	
221	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
222	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
223	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
224	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
225	
226	## POSITIONS and FACTS
227	
228	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
229	
230	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
231	
232	## The gap ledger
233	
234	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
235	
236	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
237	
238	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
239	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
240	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
241	
242	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
243	
244	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
245	
246	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
247	
248	## Reading the record
249	
250	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
251	
252	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
253	
254	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
255	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
256	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
257	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
258	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
259	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
260	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
261	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
262	
263	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
264	
265	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

272	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
273	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
274	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
275	  - what it means for the work;
276	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;

294	
295	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no note.
296	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
297	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
298	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
299	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
300	
301	## The repository's history
302	
303	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
304	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
305	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
306	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
307	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
308	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
309	# The library
310	
311	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
312	
313	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
314	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
315	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
316	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
317	
318	## How loops and reductions call the library
319	
320	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
321	
322	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
323	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
324	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
325	
326	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
327	
328	## The curator's decisions on the library
329	
330	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
331	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
332	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
333	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
334	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
335	
336	## Designing a change
337	
338	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
339	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
340	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
341	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
342	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
343	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
344	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
345	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
346	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
347	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
348	
349	## Editing
350	
351	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
352	# The specification
353	
354	Three folders hold the team's specification:
355	
356	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
357	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
358	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
359	
360	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
361	
362	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
363	
364	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
365	
366	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
367	
368	## Changing the text: the revision form
369	
370	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
371	
372	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
373	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
374	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
375	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
376	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
377	
378	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
379	
380	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
381	
382	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
383	
384	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
385	
386	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
387	
388	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
389	
390	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
391	
392	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
393	
394	## Building it
395	
396	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
397	
398	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
399	
400	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
401	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
402	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
403	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
404	
405	## When the text and an implementation disagree
406	
407	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
408	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
409	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
410	
411	## Citing it
412	
413	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
414	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

37	### 3.1 Subscripts over an unbounded index type (row 783)
38	
39	**The team's text** (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`):
40	
41	> The above overloaded declarations are not really a valid overloading. We want to say that the type variable I extends a type, say, Index which either excludes Range[I] or is a supertype of Range[I]. However, we cannot say that because when we invoke that subscripting method, we write a[1, 2, 3] where the arguments are passed as a tuple, (1, 2, 3). If we want to use Index, we need a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type Index.
42	
43	- **Where the 124 are.** All are in generic types. The fixed instances already pass: ZZ32-indexed ones because Range excludes Number (`fsi:2183`), tuple-indexed ones because a tuple excludes every trait type (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:560`).
44	- **The text's "supertype" branch.** It would make the range overload more specific, and its result `Indexed[\E,I\]` is no `E`, so the return-type rule refuses it.
45	
46	**Probes** (dotted `pick`, over a trait `Rg[\I\]` that excludes `Index`):
47	
48	| Program | Shape | Result |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| SubBound0 | `I` unbounded: `pick(i:I)` beside `pick(r:Rg[\I\])` | refused |
51	| SubBound1 | the same with `I extends Index` | accepted |
52	| SubBound5 | `I` unbounded: `pick(r:Rg[\I\])` beside `pick(t:Triv)`, `object Triv extends Rg[\Object\]` | refused |
53	| SubBound4 | all three with `I extends Index` | accepted |
54	| SubBound3 | `extends Ix[\ZZ32,(Ixi,Ixi)\]` | "(Ixi, Ixi) does not satisfy the corresponding bound Index"; accepted with the tuple rule |
55	| SubBound2, under walk | the same | loads and runs: walk does not check a trait instance's bound |
56	
57	**S1** (`designs.py subS1`, `subscripts-index-bound.patch`, 40 edits in `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`):
58	- `trait Index end`.
59	- ZZ32 extends `Index`; Range's `excludes { Number, String, Index }`.
60	- `I extends Index` on: Indexed, DelegatedIndexed, MutableIndexed, ReadableArray, ImmutableArray, Array, both Standard…ArrayType traits, FullRange, CompactFullRange, StridedFullRange, `opr :` over a FullRange, SimpleMappedSeqIndexed, the eight scalar operators over `Array[\T,I\]`, and the component's SimpleMappedIndexed, SimpleIndexValuePairs, ReversedIndexed and SimpleReversedIndexed.
61	- BoundedRange's narrowing `atMost(n:I): FullRange[\I\]` goes (`fsi:2251`, `fss:4099`). BoundedRange cannot take the bound: Range's `truncL` and `truncR` return it (`fsi:2194-2195`), and Range must stay unbounded for `TrivialOpenRange`, which is a range of `Any` (`fsi:2226`). Without this edit there are 2 more bound errors.
62	
63	**The tuple rule (the team's "magic", read as subtyping):**
64	- Checker (`checker-tupleindex.patch`): in `TypeAnalyzer.pSubInner`, a tuple of Index types is an `Index`. Subtyping only; the exclusion side (`:560`) still says a tuple excludes `Index`.
65	- Walk (`walk-tupleindex.patch`): `FTypeTuple`'s `subtypeOf`, its `meet` with `Index`, and `excludesOther`.
66

69	| subS1b: no tuple rule | 140 | 124 gone; 73 new bound errors, all at `(ZZ32, ZZ32[, ZZ32])`: api FortressLibrary 18, api RangeInternals 14, component FortressLibrary 13, component RangeInternals 28 |

73	|---|---|---|---|
74	| S1 without walk's rule | 2 failures, `ArrayScalarExtension` and `ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary`: "Failed to find any matching overload, args = (__DefaultMatrix[\RR64,2,2\],1.0)" | 0 | both stop, rc=1, at `MicroGptFlat.fss:60` `mr = 0.0 MAX m0` |
75	| S1 with walk's rule | **0 failures** | 0 | **7 of 7, rc=0, both** |

77	- **Why walk refuses without its rule.** Walk does check the bound at a generic call: it bounds the parameter by meeting its interval with the declared bound (`EvaluatorBase`, `BoundingIntervals`), and `FTypeTuple.meet` has no case for a trait.
78	- **Who wrote the two tests.** Both are the revival's (`02d09a39f`, 2026-09-19).

322	### Question 1, consequential: where the trait `Index` stands
323	
324	**Answered: option 1**, the curator at 12:46 UTC on 2026-10-23, taking the default ("I have no way how to compare the options, so I agree with your default"); P-156 holds it. Rung B builds option 1.
325	
326	**The question.** P-156 makes a tuple of indices an `Index`. The specification's rule makes every trait except `Any` and `Object` extend `Object`, and P-42 says that `Object` holds no tuple. So `Index` cannot be an ordinary trait: if it extends `Object`, a tuple of indices becomes an `Object`. Where does `Index` stand?
327	
328	**Primer.** In Fortress every trait you declare is below `Object`, whose values are objects; tuples, functions and `()` are not objects, and only `Any` holds them (P-42; `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Tuple Types": "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than `Any`."). P-156 adds:
329	
330	    trait Index end                              (* what a subscript takes *)
331	    trait ZZ32 extends { ..., Index }
332	    trait Indexed[\E, I extends Index\] ...      (* every index parameter so bounded *)
333	    m: Array2[\RR64,0,3,0,4\]
334	    m[1, 2]                                      (* passes the pair (1, 2) at I = (ZZ32, ZZ32) *)
335	
336	For `m[1, 2]` to check, `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` must be an `Index`. But the desugaring writes `trait Index end` as `trait Index extends Object end` (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations": "every trait except `Any` and `Object` implicitly extends the trait `Object`"; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:76`, `:123-126`, which rewrites even an explicit `extends Any`). Then `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` is an `Index`, and an `Index` is an `Object`, so the pair is an `Object`, and `f(x: Object)` would take `(1, 2)`.
337	
338	**The probes' shadows did not meet it.** Both the checker's and walk's rule test "a tuple below `Index`" directly, and neither makes the pair an `Object` (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/checker-tupleindex.patch`, `walk-tupleindex.patch`): the subtype relation they built is not transitive at `Index`. Nothing in the library or the suites showed it. The planner built option 1's checker half, the desugarer keeping `Index` as written, with the exclusion side of fork 7: no site moves in either stage, and walk's suites give what they gave without it (section 4, "Rung B's checker at its defaults"). So no measurement moves with the choice.
339	
340	**The team's earlier and later word.** The proposed-features appendix wants "a type, say, `Index`" and "a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type `Index`" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`). The specification's own library declares the trait of all tuples outside `Object`: `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` (`Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:180-186`), against its own implicit-`Object` rule; the batch-19 gather left that conflict to you as gather.2, with the coordinator's default to name `Tuple` beside `Any` and `Object` when a library first declares it ("Climb batch 19, listed for his review"). The team never wrote `Index`.
341	
342	**The library's way.** No trait of the library is outside `Object` but `Any` itself (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:32` declares `trait Object extends Any`).
343	
344	**Options.**
345
